chapters.title: Chapter 5: Integrity Signals in Filings and Behaviour

lessons.title: Regulatory Footprint: SEBI Orders, Exchange Penalties and Shareholder Votes

body.text: A company's regulatory file is a behaviour record compiled by people with investigative powers you do not have. It is free, public, and almost nobody reads it.

children.text: Everything else in this course asks you to interpret what a company chose to disclose. This lesson is different. SEBI orders, stock exchange penalties, secretarial audit reports, and shareholder voting results are written by outsiders, often against the company's wishes. They are the closest thing a retail investor has to an independent character reference, and they take about twenty minutes to check.

body.caption: Where a company's regulatory footprint is recorded

cells: SEBI orders
Adjudication orders, whole-time member orders, interim directions, and settlement orders naming companies, promoters, and key executives
The orders section of the SEBI website, searchable by company name
Stock exchange penalties
Fines for non-compliance with LODR, such as delayed results, missing shareholding patterns, or an improperly constituted board
Exchange announcements; companies must disclose such actions to the exchanges promptly
Corporate Governance Report
A three-year record of non-compliance, penalties, and strictures imposed by SEBI or the exchanges, stated by the company itself
Annual report, in the Corporate Governance Report section
Secretarial audit report
An independent company secretary's report on compliance with company law and SEBI regulations, including qualifications
Annexure to the Board's Report in the annual report
Surveillance lists
Whether the stock has been placed under additional or graded surveillance measures by the exchanges
NSE and BSE surveillance sections and circulars

body.text: Start with the Corporate Governance Report, because the company has to list the penalties itself. Then verify it against the SEBI orders page. A gap between what the company reports and what the regulator has published is itself a finding.

children.text: Not All Regulatory Events Mean the Same Thing
A late filing fine and a debarment order both appear in the same section of an annual report. They are not remotely the same signal. Use this ladder to place whatever you find.

body.caption: The severity ladder for regulatory events

cells: 1. Procedural lapse
Exchange fine for filing results or a shareholding pattern a few days late, typically a few thousand rupees per day of delay
Note it. One instance is administrative sloppiness; a repeated pattern suggests weak compliance culture
2. Structural non-compliance
Board without the required number of independent directors, or an improperly constituted audit committee, attracting continuing fines
More serious: the safeguards in Chapter 3 are literally not in place
3. Disclosure violation
Failure to disclose a material event, a related party transaction, or promoter encumbrance on time
Investors were denied information they were entitled to; check what was hidden and for how long
4. Conduct finding against the company
Monetary penalty or disgorgement for misstatement, fund diversion, or manipulative trades
Serious. Read the full order, not the headline
5. Conduct finding against promoters or KMP personally
Insider trading penalties, or directions restraining named individuals from the securities market or from holding board positions
The most serious for a minority shareholder, because the people running your company are the subject

body.text: Many matters end in a settlement order, where a party pays a settlement amount without admitting or denying the findings. Do not treat a settlement as an acquittal, and do not treat it as a conviction either. Read what conduct was alleged, and ask whether the company has changed anything since.

children.text: How to Read a SEBI Order

body.caption: Seven questions to ask of any order you find

cells: Who is named?
The company alone, or promoters, directors, and the CFO personally
What period does it cover?
Old conduct under a previous management is different from recent conduct under the current team
What was the conduct?
A missed deadline, or diversion of funds, misstatement, or trading on unpublished information
Contested, settled, or admitted?
Tells you how management responded when challenged
What is the remedy?
A monetary penalty is lighter than disgorgement, which is lighter than debarment from the market
Was it appealed, and what happened?
Check the Securities Appellate Tribunal outcome before drawing conclusions
Is it one event or a pattern?
Repetition across years is the single most useful thing in the file

children.text: Two examples show the range. In 2018, SEBI barred Price Waterhouse network firms from auditing listed companies for two years over the Satyam audits, an action against a firm rather than a company, which changed auditor behaviour across the market. Separately, in 2017 SEBI ordered Reliance Industries to disgorge about ₹447 crore with interest over trades in shares of a group company conducted a decade earlier, and barred it from the derivatives segment for a year. The company contested the order, and the Securities Appellate Tribunal upheld it in 2023. A large, profitable company can carry a regulatory finding without the business being in doubt, and the penalty size may be small relative to profits. What you are reading the order for is conduct, not the rupee amount.

body.title: What a Late Filing Really Costs
body.prompt: A company files its quarterly results 42 days after the deadline. The exchange levies a fine of ₹5,000 per day of delay, plus GST, which you can ignore. What is the fine in rupees?
body.explanation: 42 × ₹5,000 = ₹2,10,000. For a company earning hundreds of crores, that is nothing, and that is exactly the point. The fine is not the damage. A company that could not produce audited numbers on time, or chose not to, is telling you something about its systems or its willingness to be seen. Track the reason for the delay, not the rupee value of the penalty.

children.text: The most useful way to use this data is to count regulatory events per year across five years, for the company and for a couple of its listed peers. Here are two illustrative companies of similar size in the same industry.

body.title: Regulatory events per year: penalties, orders, and disclosed non-compliances

children.text: Company A has two minor events in five years. Company B averages four a year and the count is rising. Even if every one of Company B's events is individually small, twenty regulatory events in five years describes an organisation that treats compliance as optional. That is a management quality finding, and it usually shows up in other places later.
Shareholder Votes: The Market's Own Verdict

You met voting results in Lesson 8. Used across several years and several resolution types, they become a governance dashboard. Institutional investors employ analysts and follow proxy advisory recommendations from firms such as IiAS, InGovern, and SES, so a heavy institutional vote against a resolution is a considered judgement by people who have read the same documents you have.

body.caption: What a large institutional vote against tells you, by resolution type

cells: Reappointment of a director
Concerns about independence, tenure, attendance, or accountability for past failures
Executive remuneration
Pay seen as excessive relative to profits, peers, or performance
Material related party transaction
Doubt about arm's length pricing or the business rationale
Preferential issue or warrants
Concern about cheap control or dilution, as in the last lesson
Appointment of auditors
Questions about independence, tenure, or the firm's capability

body.text: Also watch for resolutions that are withdrawn before the vote, or revised after proxy advisers publish a negative recommendation. A company that listens and changes course is showing you a functioning governance process. A company that pushes an opposed resolution through on promoter votes is showing you the opposite.

body.title: Material Events
body.textWithBlank: Under SEBI's disclosure rules, an action taken against a listed company by a regulatory, statutory, or enforcement authority is a material event and must be disclosed to the stock ___.
body.explanation: Regulatory actions, fines, and strictures have to be disclosed to the exchanges promptly, not saved for the annual report. That is why setting an alert on your holdings' corporate announcements catches these events when they happen rather than a year later.

body.title: Noise vs Signal in the Regulatory File

columns.label: Usually Noise
points: A single late filing, explained and not repeated
An old order about conduct under a previous management, since resolved
An industry-wide regulatory change that caught many companies at once
A small technical fine disclosed promptly by the company itself

columns.label: Real Signal
points: Repeated penalties for the same lapse year after year
Orders naming promoters or key executives personally
Findings about disclosure, use of funds, or trading rather than paperwork
Qualifications in the secretarial audit report
Rising institutional votes against board, pay, or related party resolutions

body.title: Rank the Regulatory Events
body.question: Four events appear in four different companies' files. Which is the most serious signal about management quality?
options: An exchange fine of ₹3.6 lakh for filing the shareholding pattern nine days late, disclosed by the company the same week
A SEBI settlement order in which the company paid a settlement amount for a disclosure lapse dating to a merger six years ago, under a management that has since left
A SEBI order restraining the managing director and the CFO from holding any board position in a listed company, over misuse of funds raised from investors, currently under appeal
A GST demand of ₹40 crore disclosed as a contingent liability, which the company is contesting, with its legal position explained
body.explanation: Option C names the two people who run the company, concerns misuse of investor money rather than paperwork, and carries a remedy severe enough to remove them from boards. That it is under appeal matters for the final legal outcome, not for your assessment of risk today. The others are a procedural fine, old conduct under a departed management, and an ordinary contested tax demand.

body.title: Building the File on a Small Cap
body.scenario: You are considering a small cap chemicals company that screens well: 24% ROCE, low debt, three years of 30% profit growth. Its regulatory file shows exchange fines in four of the last five years for late filing of results and shareholding patterns; a fine for not having the required number of independent directors for two quarters in FY24; a SEBI adjudication order in FY25 penalising the company and two promoters for delayed disclosure of promoter share encumbrance; a secretarial audit report carrying a qualification about delayed filings with the Registrar of Companies; and 46% of public institutional votes cast against reappointing the promoter-MD at the last AGM. The stock has also been placed under short-term additional surveillance twice.
body.prompt: The financial metrics look excellent. How should the regulatory file change your decision?
body.modelAnswer: The financials describe the business; the regulatory file describes the people running it. Here the file is consistent and negative. Late filings in four of five years is not an accident, it is a system. Operating without the required independent directors for two quarters means the board and audit committee safeguards that approve related party transactions were not properly in place, which weakens every other governance check. The SEBI order on delayed encumbrance disclosure is a disclosure violation naming the promoters personally, and encumbrance is exactly the risk from Chapter 2, so check the current pledge level immediately. The secretarial audit qualification confirms the pattern independently. And 46% institutional opposition to the promoter-MD shows that professional investors reading the same file reached the same conclusion. None of this proves the 24% ROCE is false. It does mean you cannot rely on it without verification: read the related party note, check cash conversion, and track the pledge trend. Then either demand a much larger margin of safety or pass. High reported returns combined with a weak compliance culture is the profile most likely to end in an unpleasant surprise.

body.title: Build the Regulatory File for One Holding
steps: Search the company name on the SEBI orders page and list every order from the last five years, noting who is named and what the conduct was
For each, check whether it was contested, settled, or appealed, and look for the Securities Appellate Tribunal outcome
Read the penalties and strictures section of the Corporate Governance Report in the last three annual reports and compare it with what you found on the SEBI site
Read the secretarial audit report for qualifications or observations
Search exchange announcements for fines, surveillance measures, and any regulatory action disclosed during the year
Pull the voting results for the last three AGMs and note public institutional votes against board, pay, related party, and issuance resolutions
Count total events per year for five years and compare with two listed peers of similar size

body.text: Regulatory matters described here are summarised from public orders and reports, some of which have been appealed, settled, or modified. Nothing here is a finding of wrongdoing by any person or entity beyond what those public records state, and nothing here is a recommendation to buy or sell any security, or legal advice.

points: SEBI orders, exchange penalties, the Corporate Governance Report, the secretarial audit, and surveillance lists give you an outsider's record of how a company behaves
Place every event on the severity ladder: procedural lapse, structural non-compliance, disclosure violation, conduct finding against the company, conduct finding against individuals
Read each order for who is named, the period, the conduct, whether it was contested or settled, the remedy, the appeal outcome, and whether it is part of a pattern
Penalty size is a poor guide: a ₹2.10 lakh fine for a 42 day delay in results tells you about systems, not about money
Counting regulatory events per year over five years against peers exposes a weak compliance culture better than any single event
Heavy institutional votes against directors, pay, related party deals, or preferential issues are considered verdicts from investors reading the same filings
